n: After reflection he declares that the righteous and wise, and all their deeds, are in God’s hands. No one can tell from outward circumstances whether God favors them.
The same fate — death — comes to everyone: righteous and wicked, worshipers and non-worshipers, honest and dishonest alike.

f.g: One who swears oaths carelessly, compared to one who respects them.

n: It seems wrong that everyone shares one end, and that people’s hearts are full of evil and madness during life before they die.
As long as a person is alive there is hope. A living dog — a despised animal — is better off than a dead lion, the king of beasts.

f.w: a living dog is better than a dead lion
f.g: Dogs were scorned scavengers in Israel; lions symbolized power.

n: The living at least know they will die, but the dead know nothing more of this world and have no further earthly reward. Latter-day scripture teaches that the spirit lives on (Alma 40:11-14); the Preacher speaks of life “under the sun.”

f.w: the dead know not any thing

n: Their love, hatred, and envy are gone, and they no longer share in anything that happens on earth.
So go and enjoy your food and wine with a glad heart, for God approves of your living joyfully and gratefully.

f.g: God has already approved such joyful, grateful living.

n: Always wear clean, white clothes and fragrant oil — signs of festivity and gladness in the ancient world.

f.g: Scented oil worn on happy occasions.

n: Enjoy life with the wife you love throughout your brief life. Married love is one of God’s great gifts and your true portion.

f.w: Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest

n: Whatever you do, do it with all your strength, because opportunities to work and learn in mortal life end at death.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead.

n: Success doesn’t always go to the fastest, strongest, wisest, or most skilled. Unforeseen events and timing affect everyone.

f.w: the race is not to the swift

n: No one knows when misfortune will strike. Like fish caught in a net or birds in a trap, people are often caught suddenly by hard times.

f.g: The time of his calamity or death.

n: He shares an example of wisdom that impressed him deeply.
A powerful king besieged a small city with few defenders, building great siege works against it.
A poor but wise man in the city saved it by his wisdom — yet afterward no one remembered him.
Wisdom is better than strength, yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised and his advice ignored. People often value status over sound counsel.
The quiet words of the wise deserve more attention than the shouting of a ruler over fools.
Wisdom is better than weapons, but a single sinner can undo a great deal of good.
